title: ASC 606 Five-Step Revenue Recognition Model - Detailed Framework
learning_objectives: Understand the conceptual foundation of the five-step model
Apply each step systematically to revenue recognition scenarios
Identify the key decisions and judgments required at each step
Master the flow from contract identification through revenue recognition

common_question_types: Multiple choice testing understanding of each step
Identification of which step is relevant to a given issue
Ordering questions about the sequence of steps

model_overview.core_principle: Recognize revenue to depict the transfer of promised goods or services to customers in an amount that reflects the consideration to which the entity expects to be entitled.

five_steps.title: Identify the contract(s) with a customer
five_steps.key_question: Is there an enforceable agreement with a customer?

five_steps.title: Identify the performance obligations in the contract
five_steps.key_question: What distinct goods or services has the entity promised to transfer?
five_steps.primary_focus: Determining what is being sold separately

five_steps.title: Determine the transaction price
five_steps.key_question: How much consideration does the entity expect to receive?

five_steps.title: Allocate the transaction price to the performance obligations
five_steps.key_question: How should the total consideration be split among promises?
five_steps.primary_focus: Distribution based on standalone selling prices

five_steps.title: Recognize revenue when (or as) each performance obligation is satisfied
five_steps.key_question: When does the customer obtain control of the promised goods or services?

sequential_nature.description: Steps must be completed in order, and conclusions at early steps affect later steps
examples: If no contract exists (Step 1), remaining steps are not performed
Performance obligations identified in Step 2 determine how transaction price is allocated in Step 4
Transaction price determined in Step 3 is the amount allocated in Step 4
Allocation in Step 4 determines the amounts recognized as each PO is satisfied in Step 5

iterative_reassessment.principle: Entities must update their assessments at end of each reporting period
examples: Progress toward satisfaction of performance obligations updates (Step 5)
Contract modifications may require re-evaluation of all steps

step_1_detailed.title: Step 1: Identify the Contract with a Customer
step_1_detailed.definition: A contract is an agreement between two or more parties that creates enforceable rights and obligations. Contracts can be written, oral, or implied by an entity's customary business practices.

five_criteria.criterion: 1. Approval and commitment by the parties
five_criteria.detailed_explanation: All parties have approved the contract (in writing, orally, or per customary business practices) and are committed to perform their respective obligations.
assessment_considerations: Look for mutual assent - both parties agree to terms
Commitment can be demonstrated through actions, not just written documents
For oral contracts, look for evidence of agreement (emails, partial performance, etc.)
Customary business practices can create enforceable contracts even without explicit agreement
cpa_exam_tips: Don't assume a contract must be written - oral and implied contracts qualify
Look for mutual commitment - one-sided arrangements don't meet this criterion
Preliminary negotiations or letters of intent typically don't show commitment

examples.scenario: Vendor submits proposal; customer signs acceptance form
examples.explanation: Written approval demonstrates commitment

examples.scenario: Customer places order via phone; vendor begins work
examples.explanation: Oral agreement with performance demonstrates commitment

examples.scenario: Parties exchange non-binding letter of intent
examples.explanation: Non-binding agreement lacks commitment

five_criteria.criterion: 2. Each party's rights regarding goods or services are identifiable
five_criteria.detailed_explanation: The entity can identify what goods or services each party is entitled to receive or provide under the contract.
assessment_considerations: Rights need not be specified in extreme detail, but must be identifiable
Look for clear indication of what is being transferred and to whom
If goods/services are not yet specified, may still meet criterion if process for specification is clear
This criterion focuses on 'what' is being transferred, not 'when' or 'how much'
cpa_exam_tips: This criterion is typically met if customer and vendor both understand what is being bought/sold
Don't confuse with performance obligation identification (Step 2) - this is simpler
Framework agreements without specific goods/services identified may not meet criterion until orders are placed

examples.scenario: Contract to deliver 1,000 units of Product X to Customer Y
examples.explanation: Clear identification of goods and recipient

examples.scenario: Master service agreement with no specific services ordered yet
examples.explanation: Rights not identifiable until specific services are ordered

five_criteria.detailed_explanation: The entity can identify the payment terms for the goods or services to be transferred.
assessment_considerations: Payment terms need not be fixed amounts - variable pricing is acceptable
Must be able to determine how payment will be calculated
Timing of payment must be identifiable
If prices are 'to be determined,' assess whether there is a framework for determination
cpa_exam_tips: Variable consideration doesn't prevent meeting this criterion - just need to know how it's calculated
Time and materials contracts meet this criterion if rates and method are specified
Open price terms (market price at delivery) can meet criterion if market is identifiable

examples.scenario: Contract price: $100,000, due within 30 days of delivery
examples.explanation: Fixed price and timing clearly identified

examples.scenario: Contract price: $50/hour for time worked, invoiced monthly
examples.explanation: Variable amount but payment terms are identifiable

examples.scenario: Price to be negotiated in good faith upon completion
examples.explanation: No framework for determining payment amount

five_criteria.detailed_explanation: The contract must have commercial substance - that is, the risk, timing, or amount of the entity's future cash flows is expected to change as a result of the contract.
assessment_considerations: This criterion is designed to exclude sham transactions
Look for economic reality - is there a genuine business purpose?
Transactions that merely shift cash between parties without economic substance fail this test
Most normal business contracts easily meet this criterion
cpa_exam_tips: This criterion is rarely the issue in CPA exam questions
If transaction seems designed only for accounting manipulation, question commercial substance
Related party transactions may warrant closer scrutiny

examples.scenario: Entity sells products to customer for profit
examples.explanation: Clear economic substance - entity generates revenue and cash flows

examples.scenario: Two entities swap identical assets at identical prices solely to generate revenue
examples.explanation: No change in risk, timing, or amount of cash flows - sham transaction

five_criteria.criterion: 5. It is probable that the entity will collect substantially all consideration
five_criteria.detailed_explanation: It is probable (likely to occur) that the entity will collect the consideration to which it will be entitled in exchange for the goods or services transferred to the customer.
assessment_considerations: 'Probable' means likely - generally interpreted as greater than 50-75% likelihood
'Substantially all' means the amount to which entity is entitled - not necessarily the stated contract price
Focus on customer's ability AND intention to pay
Consider customer's creditworthiness, payment history, and current financial condition
Consider whether entity can stop transferring goods/services if customer doesn't pay

important_nuances.nuance: Substantially all = amount entity is entitled to
important_nuances.explanation: If entity offers price concession, collectibility is assessed on the reduced amount, not original price
important_nuances.example: Contract price $100K, but entity expects to accept $80K due to customer's financial difficulties. Assess collectibility of $80K, not $100K.

important_nuances.explanation: Criterion is evaluated when contract is entered. Subsequent deterioration in customer creditworthiness doesn't invalidate the contract.
If there is a significant change in facts and circumstances, reassess whether contract still meets criteria.

cpa_exam_tips: This is often the 'trick' criterion in exam questions
If customer's creditworthiness is questionable, this criterion may not be met
Don't confuse with revenue recognition - even if contract exists, bad debts are recorded separately
If criterion not met, receipt-based accounting may apply (recognize revenue when payment received)

examples.scenario: Established customer with strong credit history orders goods
examples.explanation: Probable that entity will collect based on customer's history

examples.scenario: Customer in bankruptcy proceedings places large order
examples.explanation: Not probable that entity will collect given customer's financial distress

examples.scenario: New customer with weak financials, but entity has right to reclaim goods if not paid
examples.explanation: Entity may still be entitled to substantially all consideration through reclamation rights

when_criteria_not_met.general_rule: If contract does not meet criteria, do not recognize revenue until either:
conditions: The criteria are subsequently met, OR
Entity has no remaining obligations and has received substantially all consideration (recognize revenue at that point)

received_consideration_before_criteria_m.accounting: Recognize consideration received as a liability (contract liability or deposit)
received_consideration_before_criteria_m.example: Customer pays $50K deposit but entity determines collectibility of remaining $200K is not probable. Record $50K as liability, don't recognize revenue yet.

reassessment.description: Reassess whether contract criteria are met if facts and circumstances change
reassessment.example: Customer's financial condition improves; collectibility now probable. Contract criteria now met; begin applying remaining steps.

contract_combinations.principle: Multiple contracts entered into at or near same time with same customer may need to be combined and accounted for as a single contract
contract_combinations.combination_criteria: Combine if ANY of the following:
criteria: The contracts are negotiated as a package with a single commercial objective
The amount of consideration to be paid in one contract depends on the price or performance of the other contract
The goods or services promised in the contracts are a single performance obligation

examples.scenario: Entity signs two contracts on same day: Contract A for product at $80K (normally $100K) and Contract B for service at $50K (normally $40K). Total consideration $130K equals combined standalone prices.
examples.explanation: Discount on Contract A offset by premium on Contract B suggests single commercial objective. Likely negotiated as package.
examples.accounting_impact: Treat as single contract with transaction price of $130K

examples.scenario: Software license contract provides discount if customer also purchases consulting contract within 30 days. Customer signs both simultaneously.
examples.explanation: Consideration in consulting contract (discount) depends on license contract. Negotiated as package.
examples.accounting_impact: Combine and allocate total consideration across all performance obligations

contract_combinations.cpa_exam_tip: Look for evidence of interdependence between contracts - pricing affecting each other, negotiated together, or goods/services that are integrated.

step_2_detailed.title: Step 2: Identify the Performance Obligations in the Contract
step_2_detailed.definition: A performance obligation is a promise in a contract with a customer to transfer a good or service (or a bundle of goods or services) that is distinct.

explicit_promises: Goods or services explicitly stated in contract
implicit_promises: Goods or services implied by entity's customary business practices, published policies, or specific statements
Example: Free shipping is implied if entity's practice is to always ship at no charge
excluded_promises: Activities that don't transfer goods or services to customer (e.g., setup activities, administrative tasks)
Immaterial promises in context of contract

distinct_determination.overview: A good or service is distinct if BOTH of the following criteria are met. Both are required - meeting only one is insufficient.

criterion_1.title: Capable of being distinct
criterion_1.description: The customer can benefit from the good or service either on its own or together with other resources that are readily available to the customer.
criterion_1.key_test: Can the customer use, consume, or sell the good or service to obtain economic benefit without the other promised goods or services in the contract?
readily_available_resources_include: Goods or services the customer has already obtained from the entity
Goods or services from other entities
indicators_of_capable: Entity sells the good or service separately
Customer could resell the good or service on its own
Customer could use the good or service in conjunction with other readily available resources

examples.scenario: Software license where software can be installed and run by customer
examples.explanation: Customer can use software on their own to obtain benefit

examples.scenario: Specialized component that only works when integrated into larger system
examples.explanation: Customer cannot obtain benefit from component alone

examples.scenario: Equipment that requires standard installation procedures widely available
examples.explanation: Customer could hire any qualified installer (readily available resource) to obtain benefit

cpa_exam_tips: Focus on 'can benefit' - not 'will benefit' or 'prefers to benefit'
Customer's ability to benefit is the test, not their actual intention
If good/service is sold separately by entity or competitors, strong evidence it's capable

criterion_2.title: Distinct within the context of the contract
criterion_2.description: The promise to transfer the good or service is separately identifiable from other promises in the contract.
criterion_2.key_test: Is the good or service highly interdependent or highly interrelated with other goods or services in the contract such that they function as inputs to a combined output?

separately_identifiable_factors.description: Promise is NOT separately identifiable if:

factors.description: Entity provides significant service of integrating goods or services with other goods or services in contract into a bundle (combined output)
factors.example: Contractor integrates design, engineering, procurement, and construction services to deliver completed building. Each service is an input to combined output.

factors.description: One or more goods or services significantly modify or customize another good or service in the contract
factors.example: Software customization services significantly modify the software license to meet customer's unique needs. Software and customization are highly integrated.

factors.description: Goods or services are highly interdependent or highly interrelated - entity couldn't fulfill promise to transfer one good/service without the other(s)
factors.example: Specialized equipment and installation where equipment is designed specifically for customer's facility and cannot function without the specialized installation.

examples.scenario: Standard laptop + routine setup service (load software, configure settings)
examples.explanation: Setup doesn't significantly modify laptop; laptop and setup aren't highly interdependent. Customer receives two separate outputs: laptop and setup service.

examples.scenario: Custom manufacturing equipment + specialized installation that adapts equipment to customer's production line
examples.explanation: Installation significantly customizes equipment; equipment and installation are highly interdependent. Customer receives one combined output: functioning production line component.

examples.scenario: Design and construction of custom facility
examples.explanation: Entity provides significant integration service combining design and construction into completed building. Customer contracts for one combined output.

examples.scenario: Off-the-shelf software license + training on how to use software
examples.explanation: Training doesn't modify software; software and training aren't highly interdependent. Customer receives software and knowledge as separate outputs.

cpa_exam_tips: This criterion is about integration and interdependence - are items combined into a unified output?
Ask: What is customer really contracting for - multiple separate things or one integrated thing?
Complex, customized projects often have one PO; standard products with services often have multiple POs
If entity is significantly integrating items, likely one PO; if just transferring multiple items, likely multiple POs

both_criteria_required.principle: An item is distinct (and therefore a separate performance obligation) ONLY if it meets BOTH criteria

decision_tree.question: Is it capable of being distinct?
decision_tree.if_no: NOT distinct → Bundle with other promises until bundle is distinct

decision_tree.question: Is it distinct within context of the contract?
decision_tree.if_no: NOT distinct → Bundle with other promises until bundle is distinct

series_of_distinct_goods_or_services.principle: A series of distinct goods or services that are substantially the same and have the same pattern of transfer can be treated as a single performance obligation
criteria_for_series: Each distinct good or service in the series meets criteria to be a performance obligation satisfied over time
Same method would be used to measure entity's progress toward satisfaction of each distinct good or service in the series

examples.scenario: Daily cleaning services for one year
examples.analysis: Each day of cleaning is distinct and satisfied over time with same progress measure
examples.treatment: Can treat as single performance obligation (series) rather than 365 separate POs
examples.benefit: Simplifies accounting while achieving same result

examples.scenario: Monthly payroll processing services
examples.analysis: Each month's processing is distinct, satisfied over time, same measure of progress
examples.benefit: Recognize revenue monthly using time-based measure

series_of_distinct_goods_or_services.cpa_exam_tip: Series provision is practical expedient. If not used, would account for hundreds of individual POs with same result. Series treatment is preferred and simpler.

equipment_plus_installation.scenario: Sale of equipment with installation services
analysis_factors: Can customer benefit from equipment without installation? (Criterion 1)
Does installation significantly modify or customize equipment? (Criterion 2)

typical_outcomes.explanation: Equipment capable of being distinct (customer could hire any installer), and installation doesn't significantly modify equipment

typical_outcomes.situation: Custom equipment + complex installation that adapts equipment
typical_outcomes.explanation: Installation significantly customizes equipment and creates combined output

outcomes.description: Assures product complies with agreed-upon specifications
outcomes.result: NOT a separate performance obligation (account for under ASC 460 as loss contingency)
indicators: Warranty covers defects existing at time of sale

outcomes.description: Provides service beyond assurance of compliance
indicators: Customer has option to purchase warranty separately
Warranty provides additional services (e.g., maintenance, upgrades)
Warranty covers issues arising after sale

license_plus_other_goods_or_services.scenario: License of intellectual property with other goods or services
analysis_factors: Do other goods or services significantly modify or customize the IP? (Criterion 2)

typical_outcomes.situation: Software license + implementation services that configure (but don't modify) software
typical_outcomes.explanation: Software capable of being distinct, and implementation doesn't significantly modify it

typical_outcomes.situation: IP license + significant development services to customize IP for customer
typical_outcomes.explanation: Development services significantly modify IP, creating combined output

immaterial_promises.principle: Entities need not assess whether promised goods or services are performance obligations if they are immaterial in the context of the contract with the customer
immaterial_promises.context: Materiality assessed at contract level, not entity level
examples: Free shipping on product sale (if shipping cost is small relative to contract)
Free gift with purchase of nominal value
Complimentary service add-on with negligible cost
immaterial_promises.cpa_exam_tip: If exam problem doesn't mention a promise or describes it as 'incidental,' treat as immaterial and exclude from PO analysis

step_3_detailed.title: Step 3: Determine the Transaction Price
step_3_detailed.definition: The transaction price is the amount of consideration to which an entity expects to be entitled in exchange for transferring promised goods or services to a customer, excluding amounts collected on behalf of third parties.

transaction_price_formula.formula: Transaction Price = Fixed Consideration + Variable Consideration (estimated and constrained) ± Time Value of Money Adjustments + Noncash Consideration - Consideration Payable to Customer
transaction_price_formula.note: Exclude amounts collected on behalf of third parties (e.g., sales taxes)

variable_consideration_summary.types: Discounts, rebates, refunds, credits, price concessions, incentives, performance bonuses, penalties, contingencies
variable_consideration_summary.estimation_requirement: Estimate variable consideration using either expected value or most likely amount method
variable_consideration_summary.constraint: Include in transaction price only to extent it is probable that a significant reversal in cumulative revenue will not occur when uncertainty is resolved
variable_consideration_summary.note: See file variable_consideration.json for comprehensive coverage

significant_financing_component_summary.when_exists: When timing of payments agreed upon by parties provides customer or entity with significant benefit of financing
significant_financing_component_summary.adjustment: Adjust transaction price for time value of money using discount rate that would be reflected in separate financing transaction
significant_financing_component_summary.practical_expedient: Do not adjust if period between transfer and payment is one year or less
significant_financing_component_summary.note: Adjust transaction price DOWN if customer pays significantly after transfer (entity financing customer). Adjust UP if customer pays significantly before transfer (customer financing entity).

noncash_consideration_summary.variability: If fair value varies due to form of consideration (not for other reasons), apply constraint on variable consideration
examples: Shares of stock received as payment
Goods or services received as payment (barter)

consideration_payable_to_customer_summar.definition: Cash amounts entity pays or expects to pay to customer (or to other parties that purchase entity's goods or services from customer)
consideration_payable_to_customer_summar.examples: Coupons, credits, slotting fees, co-op advertising allowances
consideration_payable_to_customer_summar.accounting: Reduce transaction price (contra-revenue) UNLESS payment is for distinct good or service from customer
consideration_payable_to_customer_summar.timing: Reduce revenue when later of: (1) entity recognizes revenue for transfer of goods/services, or (2) entity pays or promises to pay consideration

step_4_detailed.title: Step 4: Allocate the Transaction Price to the Performance Obligations
step_4_detailed.objective: Allocate transaction price to each performance obligation in amount that depicts the consideration to which entity expects to be entitled in exchange for transferring the promised goods or services
step_4_detailed.allocation_principle: Allocate based on relative standalone selling prices (SSP) of distinct goods or services underlying each performance obligation

standalone_selling_price.definition: The price at which an entity would sell a promised good or service separately to a customer
standalone_selling_price.best_evidence: Observable price when entity sells good or service separately

allocation_formula.formula: Allocated Amount = (SSP of Performance Obligation / Total SSP of All Performance Obligations) × Transaction Price
allocation_formula.note: This creates a relative allocation - discounts and premiums are spread proportionately

methods: Adjusted market assessment approach - evaluate market and estimate price customers would be willing to pay
Expected cost plus margin approach - forecast costs plus appropriate margin
Residual approach - total transaction price less sum of observable SSPs (restricted use)

variable_consideration_allocation.general_rule: Allocate using same method as fixed consideration
variable_consideration_allocation.exception: Allocate entirely to specific PO(s) if certain criteria met

discount_allocation.exception: Allocate to specific PO(s) if entity regularly sells that combination at that discount
discount_allocation.note: Exception requires observable evidence of selling pattern

changes_after_contract_inception.principle: Allocate subsequent changes to transaction price on same basis as at contract inception
changes_after_contract_inception.exception: If change relates entirely to specific PO, allocate only to that PO

step_5_detailed.title: Step 5: Recognize Revenue When (or As) the Entity Satisfies a Performance Obligation
step_5_detailed.satisfaction_principle: Entity satisfies performance obligation by transferring a promised good or service to customer
step_5_detailed.transfer_definition: Transfer occurs when (or as) customer obtains control of that good or service

control.definition: The ability to direct the use of, and obtain substantially all of the remaining benefits from, the asset
indicators: Entity has present right to payment
Customer has significant risks and rewards of ownership

timing_determination.question: Does the performance obligation meet criteria for over-time recognition?
timing_determination.if_yes: Recognize revenue OVER TIME as control transfers
timing_determination.if_no: Recognize revenue at POINT IN TIME when control transfers

over_time_criteria.description: Performance obligation satisfied over time if ANY ONE criterion is met:
criteria: Customer simultaneously receives and consumes benefits as entity performs
Entity's performance creates or enhances asset that customer controls as it is created/enhanced
Entity's performance does not create asset with alternative use to entity AND entity has enforceable right to payment for performance completed to date
over_time_criteria.note: Only one criterion needs to be met for over-time recognition

methods: Output methods - based on value transferred to customer (surveys, appraisals, milestones, units produced)
Input methods - based on entity's efforts or inputs (resources consumed, labor hours, costs incurred, time elapsed)
measuring_progress.objective: Depict entity's performance in transferring control
measuring_progress.note: Choose method that best depicts performance for each PO

point_in_time_recognition.when: Performance obligation does not meet over-time criteria
point_in_time_recognition.determination: Assess indicators of control transfer to determine point when control passes
point_in_time_recognition.indicators: Same as control indicators listed above

examples.description: Contract scope determined in Step 1 defines what promises are included in Step 2 analysis
examples.example: If two contracts combined in Step 1, all promises from both contracts are analyzed together in Step 2

examples.description: Number and nature of POs identified in Step 2 determines how transaction price is allocated in Step 4
examples.example: If equipment and installation are one PO (Step 2), combined SSP used in Step 4. If two POs, allocated separately.

examples.description: Transaction price determined in Step 3 is the amount allocated in Step 4
examples.example: If transaction price is $100K (Step 3), that $100K is allocated across all POs in Step 4

examples.description: Allocated amounts from Step 4 determine revenue to recognize as each PO is satisfied in Step 5
examples.example: If PO allocated $60K in Step 4 and satisfied over time, recognize $60K over performance period in Step 5

examples.description: Nature of PO affects timing determination in Step 5
examples.example: Service PO more likely to meet over-time criteria; product PO more likely to be point in time

reassessment_requirements.general_principle: Entities must update their assessments at each reporting date

what_to_reassess.when: If facts and circumstances change significantly
what_to_reassess.example: Customer's creditworthiness deteriorates significantly → reassess collectibility criterion

what_to_reassess.when: Generally no reassessment unless contract modified
what_to_reassess.note: PO identification is typically locked in at contract inception

what_to_reassess.example: Variable consideration estimates change → update transaction price and allocate change

what_to_reassess.method: Allocate changes on same basis as initial allocation

what_to_reassess.when: Each reporting period for over-time POs
what_to_reassess.example: Update percentage complete in cost-to-cost method → recognize cumulative catch-up adjustment

practical_application_flowchart.description: Systematic approach to applying five-step model

steps.question: Is there an agreement with a customer?

actions: List all promised goods and services
Evaluate each: capable of being distinct?
Allocate transaction price to each PO
For each PO: evaluate over-time criteria
If over time: select progress measure, calculate percentage complete, recognize revenue proportionately
If point in time: identify control transfer point, recognize full allocated amount when control transfers

multiple_choice_approach: Read question stem carefully to identify which step is being tested
For Step 1: look for key words like 'collectibility,' 'contract,' 'enforceable'
For Step 2: focus on 'distinct' criteria - both must be met
For Step 3: identify all components of transaction price
For Step 4: remember proportionate allocation based on SSP
For Step 5: test over-time criteria first; if none met, default to point in time
If question asks about 'when to recognize,' it's testing Step 5
If question asks about 'how much to recognize,' it could be testing Steps 3, 4, or 5
common_distractors: Confusing 'capable of being distinct' with 'distinct in context' - both required!
Assuming any variable consideration is included - must apply constraint
Allocating transaction price evenly instead of using relative SSP
Assuming service contracts are always over time - must test criteria
Recognizing revenue when billed instead of when control transfers
simulation_approach: Work through steps sequentially - don't skip ahead
Show your work - partial credit often available
In Excel exhibits, use formulas to show calculations
If running short on time, ensure Steps 1-3 are complete - they affect everything else
time_management: Don't spend excessive time on Step 1 - most contracts meet criteria
Step 2 (PO identification) often requires most judgment - allocate time accordingly
Steps 3-4 are often computational - move efficiently
Step 5 requires careful reading of facts - don't rush

key_takeaways: Five-step model provides systematic framework for revenue recognition under ASC 606
Steps must be completed sequentially as each affects subsequent steps
Step 1: Five contract criteria must all be met - collectibility is common issue
Step 2: Both distinct criteria required for separate PO - focus on integration and interdependence
Step 3: Estimate and constrain variable consideration carefully
Step 4: Allocate based on relative SSP - proportionate allocation
Step 5: Test over-time criteria first; if none met, recognize at point in time when control transfers
Understanding interdependencies between steps is critical for complex scenarios

memorization_aids.five_steps: I Identify Performance obligations, Determine price, Allocate, Recognize
memorization_aids.step_1_criteria: All Parties Receive Payment with Commercial substance, Probably collected
memorization_aids.step_5_over_time: Consumes, Controls creation, or Can't use elsewhere
